Empirical Research Plan  
“Tax Structure and Economic Outcomes in Developing Countries, 1990-2005”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Staggered‐adoption Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study.  

Why it fits  
• Treatment (major tax-structure reform) occurs in different calendar years across countries → natural staggered timing lends itself to DID.  
• Country-year panel allows for rich fixed effects that absorb time-invariant country factors and global shocks.  
• Recent DID estimators (Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021; Sun & Abraham 2021) correct for bias in staggered settings and easily extend to event-study graphs that reveal dynamics and pre-trends.  

Secondary/robustness designs: (i) Instrumental Variables using IMF conditionality as an instrument for reform timing; (ii) Synthetic controls for a subset of high-quality cases.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable  
Reform_{ct} = 1 if country c in year t has implemented a “structural” change that shifts the composition of taxes by at least 5 pp of total revenue toward the focal tax type (income-tax share ↑, VAT adoption, or corporate-tax rate overhaul). It remains 1 thereafter (intent-to-treat).

Control group  
• “Not-yet-treated” countries in each year serve as contemporaneous controls.  
• Countries that never reform during 1990-2005 are pure controls.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event time τ = t − T_c where T_c is the first year Reform_{ct}=1. Leads τ=–5,…,–1 capture pre-trends; lags τ=0,…,+5 capture post-effects.

No running variable (not RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of reform, treated and control countries would have evolved similarly in growth and revenue.  
• Plausibility: Developing countries often move together with commodity cycles and global shocks; including year FEs and region×year FEs plus macro controls (terms of trade, conflict, commodity prices) improves credibility.

A2. No anticipation / limited anticipation: Governments, firms, and households do not significantly change behavior more than one year before formal adoption.  
• Plausibility: Large reforms usually require legislation and administrative capacity; we will inspect and possibly trim years –2 and –1 if early behavioral changes are detected.

A3. Stable composition & SUTVA: Reform in one country does not directly affect outcomes in another (no cross-country spillovers within the short window).  
• Plausibility: Reasonable for tax changes; we will add region×year FEs to dampen any regional contagion.

A4. Reforms are not driven by unobserved shocks that simultaneously affect outcomes.  
• Plausibility weaker: Fiscal crises may trigger both reform and growth slowdowns. Addressed via IMF-program controls and IV robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation

T1. Endogenous reform timing (reverse causality).  
• Mitigation:  
  – Control for lagged GDP growth and fiscal balance.  
  – Instrument for Reform_{ct} with IMF conditionality intensity (whether the country is under a new IMF Stand-By or PRGF agreement requiring tax modernization).  
  – Event-study pre-trend tests: rejection of significant leads supports exogeneity.

T2. Concurrent policy bundles (trade liberalization, privatization) confound effects.  
• Mitigation: Include controls for other major reforms (trade-tariff average, capital-account openness, privatization proceeds).  
  – Triple-difference where possible (e.g., compare sectors more vs. less affected by VAT).

T3. Time-varying measurement error in tax data.  
• Mitigation: Cross-validate revenue shares with IMF GFS data; drop country-years with drastic revisions; cluster SEs at the country level to absorb serially-correlated noise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # high-dim FE regressions
library(did)            # Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ---------------------------------------------------------------
raw <- fread("tax_structure_panel.csv")  # hypothetical file

# 2. Variable construction ---------------------------------------------------
dt <- raw[, .(
  country, year,
  gdp_growth  = GDP_growth_rate,
  gov_rev_gdp = GovRevenue_GDP,
  income_share= IncomeTax_share,
  corp_share  = CorpTax_share,
  vat_share   = VAT_share,
  imf_prog    = IMF_program,            # 1 if IMF program active
  tot_change  = TermsOfTrade_change,
  conflict    = Conflict_dummy
)]

# define a reform: VAT adoption or ≥5pp rise in VAT share
dt[, reform := as.numeric((year >= first(year[ vat_share >= 0.05 ])) & !is.na(vat_share)),
     by = country]

# first year of reform
dt[, treat_year := min(year[reform==1]), by = country]
dt[is.infinite(treat_year), treat_year := NA]

# event time
dt[, event_time := year - treat_year]

# keep balanced window -5 to +5
dt_win <- dt[event_time >= -5 & event_time <= 5]

# 3. Main DID using C&S ------------------------------------------------------
att_cs <- att_gt(yname = "gdp_growth",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "country",
                 gname = "treat_year",
                 xformla = ~ tot_change + conflict + imf_prog,
                 data = dt)

# aggregate to ATT overall & event-study
agg_simple  <- aggte(att_cs, type = "simple")
agg_dynamic <- aggte(att_cs, type = "dynamic")

summary(agg_simple)
plot(agg_dynamic) + theme_minimal() + geom_hline(yintercept=0,lty=2)

# 4. Two-way FE (Sun & Abraham weights) as robustness ------------------------
dt[, post := (year >= treat_year) & !is.na(treat_year)]
reg_sa <- feols(gdp_growth ~ sunab(treat_year, year) + tot_change + conflict + imf_prog |
                  country + year, data = dt, cluster = "country")

iplot(reg_sa, xlab="Years relative to reform", ylab="β(τ)")

# 5. IV robustness: IMF conditionality ---------------------------------------
# first stage
fs <- feols(reform ~ imf_prog + lag(gdp_growth,1) + tot_change |
              country + year, data = dt, cluster = "country")
# second stage
iv <- feols(gdp_growth ~ 1 | reform ~ imf_prog, 
            data = dt, cluster = "country")
summary(iv)

```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Theory predicts that shifting from trade and turnover taxes toward broad-based VAT and income taxation should (i) raise revenue buoyancy and (ii) be roughly growth-neutral or mildly positive once efficiency gains outweigh compliance costs.  

Prior:  
• GDP growth: +0.3 – 0.6 pp per year in the five years after reform.  
• Government revenue/GDP: +1.5 – 2.5 pp within three years.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1: No pre-trend / parallel trends ........................................ 0.8  
C2: No spillovers / SUTVA .................................................. 0.9  
C3: No simultaneous shocks driving both reform and outcome ................. 0.4  
C4: Stable treatment definition and timing accuracy ........................ 0.9  
C5: Correct specification & common support (weights not dominated) ......... 0.8  

Overall, internal validity is reasonably strong but the endogenous timing of reforms (C3) remains the main concern; IV and extensive controls are therefore critical.
